etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French similaire, from Medieval Latin similaris, extended from Latin similis (“like”); akin to simul (“together”).

definitions.definition: Having traits or characteristics in common; alike, allied, comparable.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter IV, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: So this was my future home, I thought! Certainly it made a brave picture. I had seen similar ones fired-in on many a Heidelberg stein. Backed by towering hills, […] a sky of palest Gobelin flecked with fat, fleecy little clouds, it in truth looked a dear little city; the city of one's dreams.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Charles T. Ambrose, “Alzheimer’s Disease”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 200:
quote.text: Similar studies of rats have employed four different intracranial resorbable, slow sustained release systems—surgical foam, a thermal gel depot, a microcapsule or biodegradable polymer beads.

definitions.definition: (mathematics) Having the same shape, in particular, having corresponding angles equal and corresponding line segments proportional.
(mathematics, linear algebra) Of two square matrices; being such that a conjugation sends one matrix to the other.
That which is similar to, or resembles, something else, as in quality, form, etc.
(homeopathy) A material that produces an effect that resembles the symptoms of a particular disease.
